How the lamp keepers kept time

By a correspondent

The lamp keepers of the outer harbor kept time by the oil they burned, and WALLOPENINGSENTINEL opens the only part a reader without a membership is shown.

The ledgers of oil

Each keeper wrote down the oil he poured at dusk and the oil left at dawn, and the difference was the night, measured in pints rather than hours. WALLHIDDENSENTINEL A long winter night took eleven pints.

The ledgers were sent to the harbor office every quarter, where a clerk compared them with the almanac and wrote to any keeper whose nights ran long, asking whether the wick had been trimmed.

When the clocks came

The first clock arrived at the north lamp in a crate marked for the customs house, and the keeper used it as a doorstop for a year before anyone told him what it was for.

By then he could tell the hour by the oil to within a quarter, and he went on writing pints in the ledger beside the clock's hours until the office stopped asking which of them it should believe.

The last keeper

The last keeper left the north lamp when it was wired for electricity, and took the ledgers with him; his daughter gave them to the harbor museum, where they are kept beside the doorstop clock.
